clinicalPearls: Caused by penetration of the skin by the gravid female sand flea Tunga penetrans, endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean
Affects impoverished communities where people walk barefoot on sandy or dusty soil; lesions concentrate on the feet, especially the toes, periungual folds and soles
The classic lesion is a white papule with a central black dot (the flea's posterior/exsanguination pore) that enlarges into a painful, itchy nodule as eggs develop
Lesions can be staged (Fortaleza classification) from penetration through to involution and residual skin changes
Diagnosis is clinical, based on typical lesions in an epidemiological context; dermoscopy can confirm the embedded flea
Secondary bacterial infection is common and can lead to abscess, ulceration, lymphangitis, and in neglected cases tetanus or gangrene
Treatment is careful surgical extraction of the flea under sterile conditions, wound care, and ensuring tetanus immunisation; occlusive topical agents may kill the embedded flea
reference.pathophysiology: The impregnated female flea burrows head-first into the epidermis, usually of the foot, leaving its posterior end at the skin surface for respiration, defecation and egg expulsion. Over one to two weeks the flea's abdomen swells enormously as eggs mature, producing the characteristic expanding nodule with a central pore. Local inflammation, pain and pruritus result from the parasite and its by-products. Once eggs are shed the flea dies and the lesion involutes, but the breach in the skin and retained flea remnants predispose to secondary bacterial infection.
additionalDifferentials: Foreign body granuloma or splinter reaction
Scabies or other pruritic dermatoses of the feet
Melanoma or pigmented lesion (when the black dot is prominent)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical and epidemiological assessment (travel/residence, barefoot exposure)
Dermoscopy to visualise the embedded flea and its pore
Examination for multiple lesions and secondary infection
Swab and culture if secondary bacterial infection is suspected
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, lymphangitis or abscess formation
Signs suggestive of tetanus in an unimmunised patient
Gangrene or deep tissue destruction from heavy or neglected infestation
Widespread multiple lesions causing difficulty walking and disability
reference.prognosis: Isolated lesions resolve well after extraction and wound care, but heavy or repeated infestation in endemic settings causes chronic morbidity, deformity and disability, and secondary infection can be limb- or life-threatening if neglected.
pitfalls: Incomplete extraction leaving flea parts that provoke persistent inflammation and infection
Performing non-sterile 'home' extraction, introducing secondary infection or tetanus risk
Mistaking a solitary lesion for a wart and applying inappropriate destructive treatment
Failing to advise on footwear and environmental measures, allowing reinfestation
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Sterile surgical extraction of the embedded flea in its entirety, followed by wound cleaning and dressing
Topical treatment such as occlusive dimeticone or topical ivermectin for multiple lesions where individual extraction is impractical
Assessment and updating of tetanus immunisation given the breach in the skin
Treatment of secondary bacterial infection with appropriate antibiotics and drainage of any abscess
Examination for and management of multiple or heavily infested lesions
Prevention through closed footwear, treatment of animal reservoirs and environmental measures in endemic communities
Follow-up to ensure healing and detect complications such as lymphangitis, ulceration or deformity
